# Conformance corpus

This directory is a recorded conformance corpus: real `{observation,
parameters, random draw} -> intent` decisions the standard bot's compiled
script actually made, captured from `server-go/tests4bot`'s own behavioural
suite by that package's `-record` flag (`server-go/tests4bot/record_test.go`,
plan `spec/plans/publish-the-standard-bot.md` task 8).

**It is not "the suite".** It covers 30 of the suite's 41 top-level Go test
functions — 53 recorded decisions in total. The other 11 test functions
assert something about a live match, a budget, or a parameter table rather
than about what one decision decided, and recording an arbitrary decision
out of one of them would put a case in this corpus that no test actually
pins the content of. See **The count**, below, for the reasoning behind
every one of the 11, and **Why 30, not 41** for why this is the honest
number rather than a shortfall to close later.

Read this file with no Go toolchain and no checkout of
`sneat-co/chessraiders` in mind — that reader is the whole reason this
corpus exists (see **Format**, below): a creator forking
`github.com/sneat-games/chessraiders/go/bots/standardbot`, editing one
number in `params.json`, and wanting to know exactly which of these 53
decisions they just changed. It is also, potentially, the reader who matters
most for this corpus's own design: if the standard bot's Starlark runtime is
ever replaced by a plain JavaScript implementation for the trusted/common
case (the bot is a pure function of its five `decide()` arguments — the host
already resolves every legal move, so `chess-raiders-bot.star` contains zero legality
logic of its own), this corpus is the equivalence proof between the two
language implementations, not merely a creator's regression check. Every
design decision below is made with THAT reader in mind, not only a Go one.

## The count

Of `server-go/tests4bot`'s 41 top-level Go test functions:

- **30 yield at least one replayable case** — a direct call to
  `decide()`/`protocol.Decide()` whose returned `botcontract.BotIntent` the
  test's own assertions check, made with fresh (empty) bot memory, that
  completed without error. 53 distinct decisions come out of those 30 (some
  yield one case, a few yield three or four — one per difficulty in a
  table-driven loop, or one per position a test walks through).
- **11 cannot**, for one of three reasons the plan's own Approach section
  names in advance — "the ones that assert engine state, budget accounting
  or concurrency have no intent to record":

  | Test | File | Why it cannot yield a case |
  |---|---|---|
  | `TestBeaconHandOffPrefersMostAdvancedAdjacentAlly` | `beacon_handoff_test.go` | Reaches its assertion through `RunDueBots`/`runUntilWhiteActs` — a live match's own bot-turn scheduler — and checks which COMMAND the match emitted after real submission, not an isolated decision's content. |
  | `TestBeaconHandOffNeverFiresUnderLegacyRules` | `beacon_handoff_test.go` | Same as above. |
  | `TestBotKeepsOnlyOneCommandInFlight` | `convoy_test.go` | Concurrency: asserts no side ever has two charges in flight across 200 ticks of a live match; never checks what any one decision decided. |
  | `TestParamsRowCustomBreadthMustBeOverlaid` | `doctrine_params_test.go` | No bot decision at all — a parameter-table/overlay-arithmetic unit test with no engine involved. |
  | `TestBotVersusBotCommandLogGolden` | `golden_test.go` | Its own golden fixture is a whole multi-tick match command LOG, not a single decision — already covered by `testdata/bot-vs-bot-*.starlark.json`. |
  | `TestBotVersusBotRunsAreIdentical` | `golden_test.go` | Asserts that replaying a WHOLE match twice is byte-identical — the subject is match-level determinism, not one decision's content. |
  | `TestBotVersusBotRunsAreIdenticalWithSpecialists` | `golden_test.go` | Same determinism property, plus a capability check (does training emerge across several seeds) — again about the match, not one decision. |
  | `TestBotsPaceThemselvesAcrossAWholeMatch` | `golden_test.go` | Cadence/pacing invariant across a whole match. |
  | `TestCommanderReachesAMasterEngineer` | `master_engineer_test.go` | Engine-state assertion over up to 300 ticks: does a Master Engineer piece emerge, not what any single decision was. |
  | `TestSeededTieBreaksAreSlotSpecific` | `tiers_test.go` | Its own comment says it outright: "This test never calls decide() at all" — it only checks that two bot slots derive different, non-zero seeds. |
  | `TestTiersForfeitUnderATightBudget` | `tiers_test.go` | Budget accounting: the test deliberately starves the decision's budget so it forfeits — there is no valid intent to record, by design. |

This table, and the 30/41 split above it, is generated by hand from reading
every test in `server-go/tests4bot`, then checked mechanically: running
`go test ./server-go/tests4bot/ -record -v` and listing the distinct test
names under this directory reproduces exactly these 30, no more and no
fewer. Re-run that check after editing any test in the package — a test that
moves between these two buckets is exactly the kind of change this corpus
exists to catch, not to hide.

## Why 30, not 41

The plan's own Open Questions section anticipated this: *"If the honest
answer is small, the public conformance corpus is still worth shipping — a
forker with 30 recorded decisions is far better off than one with none —
but it must be labelled with its real coverage rather than presented as the
suite."* 30 of 41 (53 decisions) is that honest answer. **No behavioural
test in `server-go/tests4bot` was modified, deleted or weakened to make it
recordable** — every one of the 11 in the table above stays exactly as
written; a test that would need changing to yield a case is a finding
recorded here, not a change made to the test. The two clearest examples:

- `TestTiersForfeitUnderATightBudget` would need its budget LOOSENED to ever
  produce a successful intent to record — which defeats the exact property
  the test exists to prove.
- `TestBotKeepsOnlyOneCommandInFlight` would need to stop asserting its own
  concurrency invariant across 200 ticks and pin one decision's content
  instead — abandoning what it currently checks.

## Format

Every file here is `<TestName>.<sequence>.json` — plain JSON, `format:
"chess-bot-conformance-case/v1"`, no Go types, no reference to this
repository or any private package. A reader with `go/bots/runtime` and
`go/bots/standardbot` alone — no `facade4chess`, no `chess.State`, no
checkout of `sneat-co/chessraiders` — replays a case by feeding
`observation`, `memory`, `parameters` and `randomDraw` (each re-marshaled to
its own JSON string) into the compiled script's `decide()` entry point
exactly as `server-go/starlarktier/runtime.go`'s `CompiledTier.decide`
already does internally:

```
result := program.Call("decide", obsJSON, memoryJSON, parametersJSON, randomDrawJSON, optionsJSON)
chosenIntent := result[0] // compare against this file's own "intent"
```

That call sequence is proven complete, not assumed: the published
`go/bots/runtime`'s own `Program.call` decodes exactly `len(argsJSON)`
values and invokes the named global with nothing else in scope — its
`newThread` sets no `Print` or `Load` hook, and the only predeclared global
at all is `json` (`encode`/`decode`). A compiled script has no other way to
reach outside data, so these five fields are this case's ENTIRE input
surface, not merely the fields this corpus happened to think of.

Fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `format` | This corpus's own format tag — pin against it before trusting the shape below. |
| `paramsVersion` | `go/bots/standardbot`'s own `ParamsVersion` constant (`"chess-bot-tier-params/v1"`) — the envelope format `parameters` was resolved from, not this file's own version. |
| `script` | `{module, version}` — the exact published Go module and version (`github.com/sneat-games/chessraiders/go`, `v0.0.2` as of this writing) this case's `intent` was decided against. `go get $module@$version`, or read `https://pkg.go.dev/$module@$version`, and that release's own `go/bots/standardbot` is what ran this decision. Recorded per case, not only once for the whole corpus, so a single downloaded file stays fully informative on its own — and so a mismatch between an implementation's own replay and this file can be diagnosed as "the implementation disagrees with `$version`" rather than an open question of which `chess-raiders-bot.star` produced the recording in the first place. |
| `test` | The `server-go/tests4bot` Go test function this decision came from — provenance, not a replay input. |
| `case` | This decision's 0-based sequence within `test` — provenance, not a replay input. |
| `difficulty` | `"recruit"`, `"lieutenant"`, `"commander"` or `"custom"` — which row of `parameters` was in play, and which of `go/bots/standardbot`'s three named rows this corresponds to (`"custom"` is Commander's own row with `breadth` overlaid from the match). |
| `parameters` | The resolved parameter row — the SAME shape as one row of `go/bots/standardbot/params.json`, with Custom's `breadth` already overlaid. |
| `observation` | Everything the script's `decide()` could read for this decision — squares as algebraic strings ("e4"), every enum as its lowercase wire name. This is `decide()`'s first argument. |
| `memory` | Always `{}`. Every case here is a fresh decision — bot memory carried over from a previous decision is exactly the situation this corpus cannot capture faithfully from `{observation, parameters, random draw}` alone (see **What "replayable" excludes**, below) — so every recorded case starts from nothing. Recorded explicitly anyway, so this field plus the four around it are the complete, literal argument list. |
| `randomDraw` | The one pre-drawn random value `decide()`'s own `host_random_draw` argument received, encoded as a **decimal string** — see below for why a bare JSON number is not safe here. |
| `options` | Always `0` — every case is an ordinary bot decision, never the Adviser's explain-mode request for ranked alternatives. |
| `intent` | The decision the script returned, in the same self-describing shape as `observation` — squares as algebraic strings, enums as lowercase wire names. Compare this against your own replay's first returned value — see **Why `intent` is sometimes `null`**, just below, before writing that comparison. |

### Why `intent` is sometimes `null`

`decide()` returns Starlark's `None` as its chosen intent whenever there is
nothing worth doing this tick — `chess-raiders-bot.star`'s own `decide()` has four such
`return None, memory, []` branches, and "pass" is an ordinary, recurring
decision, not an edge case. That `None` crosses the JSON boundary as a bare
`null` — `go/bots/runtime`'s own `Program.Call` encodes it that way — so
this field is recorded as JSON `null` for exactly those cases, never as a
`{"kind":"none",...}` object: an object there would be this repository's own
internal, Go-side stand-in for "no intent"
(`server-go/botcontract.BotNoIntent()`, invented purely so a Go caller has an
ordinary struct to switch on), and a correct reimplementation's own
`result[0]` for the identical decision is `null`, not that stand-in — so the
comparison this corpus asks a reader to make must be `result[0] ==
case.intent` with no special-casing on either side. (An earlier revision of
this corpus recorded the stand-in object instead, which told a demonstrably
correct implementation it was wrong on both of this corpus's "nothing worth
doing" cases — fixed once a pre-merge review replayed all 53 cases against
the published module directly and caught the mismatch.)

### Why `randomDraw` is a string, not a number

`decide()` takes one pre-drawn random value as its fourth argument rather
than calling a random-number generator itself (`server-go/starlarktier/
rng.go`'s own `hostRandomDraw` — see that file for the full reasoning: a
fresh draw per call previously caused a livelock between two "equally good"
candidates). That value is a pure function of a seed and a revision number
that live only in the private engine's own match state — a value no
forker's browser session or Node harness has any way to derive on their
own, which is why this corpus records the DRAWN VALUE itself rather than
the seed and revision it came from (plan task 8, verbatim: *"Include the RNG
draw explicitly in each case. A recorded decision that can't be reproduced
because the random draw wasn't captured is not replayable, and the private
suite's determinism comes from a seeded source that a creator won't
have."*).

That value is masked to 63 bits (`rng.go`'s own `& 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`) and
in practice always lands far above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53-1) —
**every one of this corpus's own 53 recorded draws does**. A bare JSON
number in that range is not safe for the exact reader this corpus exists to
serve: a plain `JSON.parse()` in Node or a browser silently rounds it to the
nearest representable `double` before any `draw % count` logic in a
JavaScript reimplementation ever runs, corrupting the one value this whole
case exists to make reproducible — and the resulting mismatch would look
like a bot bug, not an encoding bug, which is a strictly worse failure mode
than an obviously-wrong number. `randomDraw` is therefore a decimal STRING:
round-trips through `BigInt(case.randomDraw)` (or an arbitrary-precision
decimal type in any other language) with no precision loss, the same reason
large integer IDs cross JSON APIs as strings elsewhere (Twitter/Discord
snowflakes). A Go reader parses it with `strconv.ParseInt(s, 10, 64)`.

**The general rule, for whoever adds the next field**: `randomDraw` is not a
one-off exception, it is this corpus's only instance so far of a rule that
applies to every field — an int64 whose real values can exceed 2^53
(`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`) is encoded as a decimal STRING, never a bare JSON
number. `observation`'s own `nowMs`, `revision`, `recoveryUntil` and each
wall's `integrity`/`maximumIntegrity` are int64 too, but stay bare numbers
today because their real magnitudes never get close (`nowMs` tops out
around `1.7e12` in this corpus, many orders of magnitude under `2^53 ≈
9e15`) — checked, not assumed, before leaving them as-is. Check a new int64
field's actual magnitude against that ceiling before deciding how to encode
it; do not assume "it's an int64" alone means it needs stringifying, and do
not assume it doesn't.

## What "replayable" excludes

A case is only recorded when three things are true of the underlying
`decide()` call, in order:

1. **It completed without error.** A decision whose budget was deliberately
   exhausted (`TestTiersForfeitUnderATightBudget`) never reaches a valid
   intent — there is nothing to replay.
2. **Bot memory going in was empty.** `decide()` genuinely reads memory
   carried over from a previous decision (a bot "remembering" the piece it
   last committed to — `convoy_test.go`'s
   `TestBotPassesWhileItsOwnPieceCharges`, past its first call). This
   corpus's own recorded shape is the three-tuple the task asks for, with
   no fourth memory field, so a decision that depended on carried memory is
   not faithfully replayable from that triple alone.
3. **It was reached directly from `server-go/tests4bot`'s own test code**
   — the shared `decide()` helper (`harness_test.go`) or a test's own
   direct `protocol.Decide()` call — **never through
   `facade4chess.Service.RunDueBots`**, the live-match bot-turn scheduler.
   Every match-based test makes real decide() calls as a side effect of
   just starting a match, whether or not that test's own assertions have
   anything to do with what got decided — recording one of those anyway
   would silently inflate this corpus with cases no test actually pins.

## Regenerating

```
go test ./server-go/tests4bot/ -record
```

regenerates every file under this directory from whatever the current suite
actually decides. Without `-record`, an ordinary `go test
./server-go/tests4bot/...` recomputes the same 53 cases and fails, naming
every file, on any byte-for-byte drift — the re-record check plan task 8
asks for, in the same two-mode shape `golden_test.go`'s own `-update`
already uses for `testdata/bot-vs-bot-*.json`.
